conservation.notes: Has a wide distribution and an increasing population trend. The New Zealand subspecies is T. s. vagans.

human_tolerance.notes: In Australia it inhabits open eucalypt forests, melaleuca swamps, mangroves, mudflats, wetlands, river and lake margins, farmland, parks and gardens. In New Zealand the subspecies vagans makes post-breeding movement downslope, from forest to coast and open land.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The breeding season runs from August to March, mostly September to January, often with two broods. Once mated, both members of the pair dig the nest, in a burrow in a river bank, a hollow in a large branch or a termite mound. The female lays 3 to 6 glossy white rounded eggs of about 25 x 22 mm, incubated 17-18 days by both parents (mainly the female); both parents, and possibly helpers, feed the nestlings for up to 4 weeks and for a further 7-10 days after fledging.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: Authored judgement on the window, informed by the sourced New Zealand behaviour: T. s. vagans shows altitudinal migration, with post-breeding movement from higher altitudes to the coast and also from forest to coast and open lands. The southern two-thirds of the Australian population instead leaves the country altogether (to New Guinea, the eastern Solomon Islands and Indonesia) from the end of the breeding season and returns in August and September; that movement is not represented here because this record describes the resident New Zealand population.

common_names.note: English, French, German and Dutch names from Wikidata P1843. The Māori name kōtare appears in the article's In culture section rather than on the Wikidata property.

range.note: Distribution and habitat section: Australia, New Zealand, Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island, New Guinea, eastern Indonesia, much of northern and western Melanesia and the Kermadec Islands. Australia (including Lord Howe), New Zealand (including the Kermadecs), Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, the Solomon Islands and Norfolk Island are ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes; New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands are carried as the ISO 3166-2 subdivision FR-NC because no alpha-2 code exists for them. Christmas Island, Malaysia, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Nauru and the Philippines are recorded in the article only as vagrants and are deliberately not listed as native.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Feeding section: 'Usually, the sacred kingfisher will sit on a low branch and wait for prey to pass by. It swoops down to grab the prey by briefly landing (sally-pounce) or hovering (sally-strike), and then returns to its perch.' Fly is the working gait; hop is included because the bird briefly lands on the ground or a low branch to take prey, and the shared program needs a short non-flight gait.

traits.nest_type.note: Breeding section: 'both members of the pair dig the nest; a burrow in a river bank, a hollow in a large branch or a termite mound are prime examples of nest location.' Burrow is the matching nest type for a dug tunnel or hollow.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 0.053 kg falls in the Small band.

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET Mass = 52.96 g, consistent with Wikipedia's 28-61 g for males and 28-56 g for females.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 28-61 g, the widest span of the two sex-specific ranges the article gives.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Honest gap. No openly licensed source consulted (English Wikipedia, Wikidata P2050, AVONET) gives a wingspan for the sacred kingfisher. Derived from AVONET's mean wing (chord) length of 91.3 mm at a factor of 2.5, giving 0.23 m; a spread wing's span runs roughly two to three times its chord, so treat this as a range estimate rather than a measurement. AVONET's Kipps distance of 27.7 mm on a 91.3 mm wing (ratio 0.30) indicates a longer, more pointed wing than the other passerines measured here, which fits the sallying, hovering flight the article describes.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap: neither the article, Wikidata nor AVONET states a typical or mean wild lifespan for this species, and the article records only that the population trend is increasing. 6 years is a judgement for a medium-sized woodland bird of this size.

traits.diet.note: Feeding section: 'a wide variety of invertebrates (particularly insects and spiders), small crustaceans, fish (infrequently), frogs, small rodents and reptiles, and there are a few reports of them eating finches and other small birds.' Invertebrates dominate; vertebrates are substantial but secondary, and the infrequent fish are folded into the single small_vertebrate resource because the schema's resource tag vocabulary has no separate fish tag. Shares derive from that ordering: invertebrate 1.0, small_vertebrate 0.6. AVONET independently classifies the species as Trophic.Level Carnivore, Trophic.Niche Invertivore.

traits.social.note: Breeding section: both members of the pair dig the nest, both parents incubate (mainly the female), and both feed the nestlings, with possible helpers. structure Pair reflects that; group_size 1-4 covers a pair, a pair with young, and the occasional helper.

traits.defense.note: Authored from the sourced behaviour: the bird drops from its perch and flies off, rather than showing any threat display. The article records no defensive display.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.2. Kingfishers are bold, low-perching birds that work right outside buildings in parks and gardens, but they do drop off the perch and fly away from a close approach.

habitat.use.note: AVONET Habitat = Woodland and Primary.Lifestyle = Insessorial; the article describes the bird sitting on a low branch and sallying to the ground or the water surface, so foraging is arboreal in origin with brief ground and water sorties. arboreal 0.9 / ground 0.1.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Breeding section: the nest is dug in a burrow in a river bank, a hollow in a large branch or a termite mound, so cavity is the matching shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Feeding section for the prey spectrum and for the low-branch watch perch the bird returns to after each strike; Breeding section for the burrow, hollow or termite-mound nest. No monthly or seasonal weighting was applied because the article describes none.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Distribution and habitat section lists 'farmland, parks and gardens' among the Australian habitats, which supports uses_gardens; the article does not state how the New Zealand population uses built-up land, so Adapter rather than Exploiter is the honest affinity. light_max and flight_distance_m are authored judgements.

seasonal.strategy.note: The New Zealand subspecies vagans stays in New Zealand all year and makes post-breeding altitudinal and habitat movement, while only the southern two-thirds of the Australian population actually leaves the country. Because this record describes the resident New Zealand population that an Auckland garden would show, ActiveYearRound is the correct strategy rather than Migration; the Australian departure is recorded in the dispersal phase note instead.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding section for the August-March season (mostly September to January), two broods, pair-dug burrow/hollow/mound nest, 3-6 white eggs of 25 x 22 mm, 17-18 day incubation and the up-to-4-week nestling period plus 7-10 days after fledging; Distribution and habitat section for the New Zealand post-breeding movement downslope and from forest to coast and open land, and for the Australian departure and return. The end of the dispersal phase is an authored judgement. The breeding phase is restricted to NZ-AUK because the Australian population has a different annual cycle.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Breeding section: 3-6 eggs, 17-18 days of incubation, nestlings fed for up to 4 weeks. duration_days is the midpoint of each sourced range (17.5 for the egg; 28 for the nestling period, which the article gives as 'up to 4 weeks').

look.note: Description section for the plumage: mostly blue-green to turquoise above, white underparts and collar feathers, a black mask and buff lores; females are usually greener, duller and less buff beneath, and juveniles have buff or mottled brown edges on the collar, underparts and upper-wing coverts. The article does not describe the bill colour, so the bill is coloured with the black mask slot as an authored choice. Proportions are authored from AVONET's measurements for this species (culmen 43.4 mm, tarsus 12.9 mm, wing 91.3 mm, Kipps distance 27.7 mm, tail 60.5 mm) read against the biped_winged body plan: a very long dagger bill about as long as the head, very short legs, a large head on a compact body, and a moderately long, more pointed wing than the other passerines here. The breast part is coloured to carry the white underparts.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. Honest limitations, stated rather than papered over: (1) the shared program has song and alarm actions and this record declares no vocalizations, because no openly licensed source consulted describes the sacred kingfisher's calls in words (the article links to recordings but does not transcribe them, Wikimedia Commons holds no audio for the species, and the Xeno-canto API this kit would use for openly licensed recordings has been retired). That leaves two UnknownCallId warnings, which is the honest gap rather than an invented call description. (2) food_tag is invertebrate because insects and spiders dominate the sourced diet; the program forages by hopping, which is a loose fit for a bird that sallies from a perch. (3) nest_m1/nest_m2 are 9 and 1 for the mostly-September-to-January breeding core, which the shared program wraps around its own hard-coded spring months. flee_m 12 and song_cooldown_s 40 are judgements for a bold, low-perching sit-and-wait predator.
